Instruments come from the app's catalogue, but every price path is synthetic: each instrument is simulated independently with the same expected return and its own volatility. Outcomes illustrate ideas from the lessons. They don't predict real returns and are not product recommendations.

stars.goalRule: no shortfall and the final value reaches the target
stars.assetsRule: money only in evaluation.suitableInstrumentIds, in at least evaluation.minInstruments of them (cash is always fine)
stars.sharesRule: every evaluation.shareRanges entry holds: the share of the budget in its instruments (plus cash when includesCash) is between min and max, inclusive; with each: true, every listed instrument's own share must be in the range instead

scenarios.title: Kuba's Safety Cushion

persona.name: Kuba
persona.situation: First job on a 6-month contract that may not be renewed. No savings cushion yet.

scenarios.goal: Pay the car repair in four months without a loss and still have a cushion at the end of the year.

traps.label: All in the world fund
traps.why: The repair may have to be paid by selling the fund after a drop, and a year is too short to recover.

traps.label: One exciting stock
traps.why: A single volatile stock can be far down exactly when the repair is due.

evaluation.explanation: The repair is due in four months and the job may not last, so most of the money belongs in cash. Up to about 30% can go into a broad fund such as the world or S&P 500 fund. Single stocks swing too much for an emergency fund.

debriefPoints: An emergency fund needs to be available, and its value shouldn't swing.
One year is too short to recover from a drop.
Cash grows slowly, but here safety matters more than growth.
notSimulated: Savings-account interest and inflation (cash earns 0% and prices don't rise in this sandbox).

scenarios.title: Lena and Tom's Wedding

persona.name: Lena and Tom
persona.situation: Wedding booked for a fixed date in 2 years. The venue is paid on that day.

scenarios.goal: Have the full wedding budget on the day.

traps.label: Spread across funds
traps.why: Diversified, but still all in shares: two years is too short to be sure of the full amount.

traps.label: One region
traps.why: All the money in one market's ups and downs, right before a fixed date.

evaluation.explanation: The wedding date is fixed and only two years away, so nearly all of the money should keep its value in cash. A small part, up to a quarter, can go into a broad world or S&P 500 fund. One region or emerging markets add risk the couple doesn't need.

debriefPoints: A fixed date close ahead calls for money that keeps its value.
Diversification lowers risk but doesn't remove it.
Growth isn't needed when the goal is to keep what you have.
notSimulated: Term deposits and bonds, which would usually fit a known date (no such instruments in the catalogue yet).

scenarios.title: Marek's Favourite Company

persona.name: Marek
persona.situation: Engineer with a stable job and an emergency fund already in place. A big fan of one chip-equipment company who wants to go all in.

traps.label: All in
traps.why: One company's problems hit the whole portfolio.

traps.label: One theme
traps.why: Looks spread out, but it is all one volatile theme, half of it in one company.

evaluation.explanation: Six years and a stable job allow mostly investing. The bulk belongs in broad funds across regions, and the favourite company fits as a small part, up to 10%. Going all in, or doubling up on tech with the NASDAQ fund, ties the money to one theme.

debriefPoints: A single stock carries the full damage of one company's problems.
A fund spreads the money across many companies.
A favourite stock fits as a small part of a long-term mix.
notSimulated: Shares moving together: in this sandbox every instrument moves independently, which makes any mix look more diversified than it really is.

scenarios.title: Zofia Only Buys What She Knows

persona.name: Zofia
persona.situation: Inherited money. A relative says to only buy big local European names you know.

traps.label: One familiar name
traps.why: Familiar isn't the same as safe: one company decides the result.

traps.label: Home only, mostly cash
traps.why: Far too cautious for 8 years, and the small invested part depends on one region.

evaluation.explanation: Eight years allow mostly investing, spread across regions rather than only at home: world, US, European and emerging-market funds. The European fund is fine as one part, up to about 40%. Familiar names like Allianz or Deutsche Telekom aren't less risky just because they're known.

debriefPoints: Diversify across companies and regions, not only within one market.
Knowing a company's name doesn't lower its risk.
Compare instruments on risk, return, liquidity, cost and horizon.
notSimulated: Fund fees (no fees in this sandbox), so the cost difference between funds isn't visible here.

scenarios.title: Olek's Group-Chat Tip

persona.name: Olek
persona.situation: Student with savings from a summer job. A group chat says one tech stock can't lose. Next semester's tuition comes out of this money in 6 months.

scenarios.goal: Pay the tuition and keep the rest.

rules.label: No single stock above 5% of money needed soon

traps.label: Trust the chat
traps.why: Tuition is due in 6 months, and the tip can be down a lot by then.

traps.label: Half on the tip
traps.why: Half of the tuition money rides on one stock.

evaluation.explanation: Half of the money pays the tuition in six months and the rest should be kept, so almost all of it stays in cash. If Olek follows the tip at all, it's a small bet of up to 5% on that one stock; a little in the world fund is the steadier choice. Other stocks would just be new bets.

debriefPoints: A tip is a bet on price, not a plan.
Never bet money you need soon.
If you speculate at all, keep it small and separate from important goals.
notSimulated: Crypto, leverage and a hype-then-crash price pattern (no such instruments or scripted events in this sandbox).

scenarios.title: Nina's Home Deposit

persona.name: Nina
persona.situation: Renting, steady job, emergency fund in place. Plans to buy a flat in 4 years.

scenarios.goal: Grow the home deposit a little without risking the purchase.

traps.label: Only cash
traps.why: Safe, but no growth at all over 4 years.

traps.label: All in shares
traps.why: A drop just before the purchase can shrink the deposit.

evaluation.explanation: Four years to the flat is a medium horizon: keep a large part, roughly 35–70%, safe in cash and invest the rest in broad funds. Single stocks and the tech-heavy NASDAQ fund put the deposit at unnecessary risk.

debriefPoints: A medium horizon needs a balance of growth and safety.
Ask the five questions for each pick: risk, return, liquidity, cost and horizon.
notSimulated: Bonds and deposits, the usual middle ground (only cash and shares in this sandbox).

scenarios.title: Paula's Uneven Income

persona.name: Paula
persona.situation: Single parent and freelance designer with irregular income. Saving for a child's school costs. A quiet spell with no clients is likely.

scenarios.goal: A school fund that survives a bad year.

moneyNeeds.label: Two quiet months with no clients

traps.label: 5 years is long
traps.why: The income gap can force a sale during a drop.

traps.label: Luxury bet
traps.why: Half on one company, with dependents and an uneven income.

evaluation.explanation: Irregular income and a child who depends on her lower Paula's capacity for risk, and a quiet spell will need €3,000 in about two and a half years. Keeping roughly a third to a half in cash covers it, and the rest can go into broad funds. A luxury-brand stock is a bet, not a school fund.

debriefPoints: Age and horizon aren't the whole picture.
Unstable income and dependents lower risk capacity, so more stays in cash.

scenarios.title: Ewa's First Salary

persona.name: Ewa
persona.situation: First full-time job, no expensive debt, emergency fund already built. Investing the first savings for the long run.

scenarios.goal: Grow as much as possible over the first 10 years.

traps.label: Play it safe
traps.why: No growth at all in 10 years of compounding time.

traps.label: All on one star
traps.why: A long horizon doesn't make one company safe.

evaluation.explanation: Ten years, a steady income and an emergency fund in place allow a growth-oriented mix: almost everything in broad funds across regions and company sizes. Cash barely grows, the NASDAQ fund leans on one sector, and a single star stock adds risk without adding expected return.

debriefPoints: A long horizon and future income allow a growth-oriented mix.
Starting early gives compounding the most time.
notSimulated: Monthly contributions and the 'start at 25 vs 35' comparison (one starting amount only, horizon at most 10 years).

scenarios.title: Sam's University Fund

persona.name: Sam
persona.situation: Steady income and two children. Saving for the eldest's university, with an older house that may need repairs.

scenarios.goal: Have the university fund ready in 7 years.

traps.label: Two favourite stocks
traps.why: Two companies decide the child's education.

traps.label: Park it in cash
traps.why: Safe, but 7 years without any growth.

evaluation.explanation: The university fund has seven years, but the house may need €5,000 of repairs in under three. A cash part of 10–40% covers surprises so the investments can stay put, and the rest goes into broad funds. Two favourite stocks are not a plan for a child's education.

debriefPoints: Each goal gets its own horizon and mix.
A cash part covers surprises so the investments can stay put.
notSimulated: Several goals in separate buckets (one portfolio per scenario).

scenarios.title: Danuta's Glide Path

persona.name: Danuta
persona.situation: Savings at their largest, retiring at 67. Has kept everything in a tech fund for years because it has done well.

scenarios.goal: Protect what's been built over the last 9 years before retirement, while still growing.

traps.label: It worked so far
traps.why: A big drop near retirement hits the largest balance.

traps.label: All to cash
traps.why: No growth at all for 9 years, with a long retirement still ahead.

evaluation.explanation: With retirement nine years away, Danuta should move gradually from growing to protecting: a large cash part, and the rest spread across broad funds in several regions. Keeping everything in one tech fund because it did well is concentration, not a plan.

debriefPoints: Shift from growing to protecting gradually.
Even near retirement, part of the money stays invested for growth.
notSimulated: A glide path that changes the mix year by year (one decision at the start), and bonds as the steadier part.

scenarios.title: Henryk Retires Next Year

persona.name: Henryk
persona.situation: Retires in a year and will live on these savings for the first years of retirement.

scenarios.goal: Pay two years of spending and keep the rest for later retirement.

traps.label: Stay fully invested
traps.why: Spending is paid by selling shares, even right after a drop.

traps.label: Two funds, no buffer
traps.why: No cash buffer: every withdrawal is a sale at that day's price.

evaluation.explanation: Withdrawals start in a year, so a cash buffer of at least two years of spending, plus a margin, avoids selling funds after a drop. The rest stays invested in broad funds for later in retirement.

debriefPoints: Sequence risk: the same drop hurts more when withdrawals start.
A cash buffer of 1-3 years of spending avoids selling at the bottom.
notSimulated: A scripted crash: the market path is random, so some runs show sequence risk more clearly than others.

scenarios.title: Ola Minds the Gap

persona.name: Ola
persona.situation: Expects a public pension of 1,800 a month against 3,000 needed: a gap of about 288,000 over 20 years of retirement. This money is the start of Ola's own retirement savings.

scenarios.goal: Grow the retirement savings as much as sensible over 9½ years.

traps.label: Only savings
traps.why: The gap doesn't shrink at all.

traps.label: Too cautious
traps.why: Most of the money does no work for almost 10 years.

evaluation.explanation: Nine and a half years and a large pension gap call for growth: most of the money in broad funds across regions and company sizes, and little in cash.

debriefPoints: Public pensions often cover only part of what's needed.
Cash alone can't close a large gap; time and compounding do most of the work.
notSimulated: Pension accounts: tax advantages, employer contributions and lock-up rules (no taxes or locked accounts in this sandbox).
